summary: No ineffective assistance was shown based on counsel's agreement to annotate the verdict sheet for readback purposes. The case was remitted for consideration of unresolved issues by the Appellate Division.
Most ineffective-assistance claims depended on matters outside the trial record and were properly left to CPL 440.10 review. Denial of defendant's postverdict DNA-testing motion was upheld.
In assessing SORA risk level, courts may consider youthful-offender adjudications. The challenged risk assessment was affirmed.
The accusatory instrument sufficiently alleged possession of a dangerous knife under the applicable facial-sufficiency standard. Dismissal was unwarranted.
Applying Taranovich factors, the Court held defendant's constitutional speedy-trial right was violated by the prosecution delay. The accusatory instrument was dismissed.
The conspiracy conviction was not supported by legally sufficient evidence on this record. The challenged count was dismissed.
Assuming suppression error, any error was harmless under Crimmins in light of the record. Remaining trial-error and prosecutorial-misconduct claims were rejected.
Any misuse of Frye procedure to address expert-foundation issues was harmless. A hearsay ruling admitting prior-threat testimony was erroneous but harmless given overwhelming proof.
The court properly refused a deadly-force justification charge where the evidence did not support the statutory prerequisites, including retreat-related limits. Conviction was affirmed.
On this record, lower-court findings that police escalation and frisk were justified under De Bour were supported and therefore beyond further review. Any Miranda-related error was harmless.
Dismissal of a noninclusory concurrent-count charge involving a BB gun fell within trial-court discretion and did not impair defendant's ability to contest the separate firearm count.
A youthful offender adjudicated for a felony sexual assault could lawfully receive a 10-year probation term. Penal Law 65.00's sexual-assault probation provision applied.
Defendant had no right to hybrid representation with standby counsel, and the trial court properly rejected that request. Related CPL 250.10 psychiatric-notice rulings were upheld.
For SORA risk factor 2, the court could assign points based on clear-and-convincing proof of sexual intercourse/deviate sexual conduct despite criminal-trial acquittals on those charges.
Appeal from local criminal court was properly dismissed where defendant failed to file a required affidavit of errors.
The Appellate Division properly entertained review of an oral suppression ruling not reduced to writing, and record support for suppression foreclosed further Court of Appeals review.
Identity-theft liability may be established by using another's identifying information as the statutory means of assuming that person's identity. Conviction was upheld.
Suppression of breath-test evidence was proper where testing occurred outside statutory compelled-test limits and purported consent was not voluntary under the circumstances.
Unlawful use of secret scientific material includes reproducing proprietary source code by copying and uploading it, even without physically removing a paper document.
Where a hearing court may have made an implied credibility finding on juror-misconduct allegations, the Appellate Division erred in reweighing the record. Matter was remitted for proper review.
The Penal Law 'place of business' weapon-possession exception is narrow and does not extend to an ordinary employee lacking ownership or principal-operating authority.
Admission of an unidentified declarant's 911 statement lacked a proper hearsay basis and was not harmless. The conviction was reversed and a new trial ordered.
Defendant failed to establish ineffective assistance based on counsel's omission of a Confrontation Clause argument, because the record did not show lack of strategic justification.
The switchblade weapon count was facially sufficient, and trial proof, including officer operability testimony and demonstration, supported the conviction.
Challenges to limitations on defense expert testimony were largely unpreserved, and the evidentiary rulings were within discretion. Ineffective-assistance and remaining claims were rejected.
Martin Act claims seeking statutory disgorgement/relief were governed by CPLR 214 (2)'s three-year limitations period. The Executive Law 63 (12) claim was remitted for further consideration.
The Appellate Division exceeded CPL 470.15 limits by affirming on a ground not decided adversely to defendant by the suppression court. Reversal and remittal were required.
Brief questioning on a represented matter was legally discrete and separable from questioning on an unrepresented matter, so suppression was unwarranted. The trial judgment was reinstated.
A defendant who pleaded guilty could not obtain CPL 440.10 relief on a freestanding actual-innocence theory under the circumstances presented. Relief was denied.

Denial of CPL 440.10 relief was upheld because alleged newly discovered third-party culpability evidence lacked sufficient admissible, independently reliable corroboration. Brady claims were also rejected.
The evidence was legally sufficient to prove depraved-indifference first-degree assault based on prolonged, brutal abuse creating a grave risk of death and showing utter indifference to life.
A Buford juror-inquiry claim was unpreserved, and the challenge to gang-related testimony lacked merit on the trial record.
Complete denial of defense summation in a bench trial violated the Sixth Amendment right to counsel. The error required reversal and a new trial.

Waiver of indictment was valid where defendant executed a written waiver in open court in counsel's presence as required by the State Constitution. No additional colloquy was constitutionally required.
Failure to provide meaningful notice of a substantive jury note under CPL 310.30 and O'Rama is a mode-of-proceedings error requiring reversal.
As in Parker, the trial court's failure to give meaningful notice of a substantive jury note required reversal; gist-level notice was insufficient and preservation was not required.
The Appellate Division's weight-of-evidence review did not apply an incorrect legal standard warranting reversal. The order was affirmed.
Whether entry into defendant's apartment was by voluntary consent was a mixed question of law and fact, and record support for the finding of consent foreclosed further review.

An accusatory instrument alleging paid 'manual stimulation' on a street corner at night sufficiently pleaded patronizing prostitution in context. Reversal and remittal were for unresolved Appellate Term issues.
A jury trial commences when jury selection begins; defendant's pro se request made near the end of selection was untimely.
No state constitutional coram nobis remedy was available to revive an untimely criminal leave application beyond CPL 460.30's one-year limit.
A jurisdictional challenge based on Family Court exclusivity was not reviewable because the underlying support order was issued by Supreme Court in a matrimonial action.

Defendant's guilty plea forfeited his CPL 190.50 (6) grand-jury witness-vote challenge because the claimed defect did not rise to a constitutional process-integrity defect surviving plea forfeiture in these circumstances.
Counterfeit event tickets can satisfy Penal Law 170.10 (1)'s catchall because tickets affect legal rights and status; second-degree forged-instrument possession charges were valid.
The proof was legally sufficient to establish serious physical injury. The conviction was affirmed.

A noncitizen defendant who shows charged offenses carry potential deportation has established sufficient additional penalty to trigger the Sixth Amendment jury-trial right for otherwise petty offenses.
Enterprise-corruption evidence was legally insufficient to prove defendant's knowing and intentional participation in the charged criminal enterprise. The indictment was dismissed.
A non-sex offense homicide conviction involving a minor victim did not make defendant a registrable 'sex offender' under New York SORA solely because another state required registration.
Defendant was not entitled to relief compelling New York correctional authorities to follow a New Jersey sentencing recommendation.
Resubmission of a previously deadlocked count required CPL 190.75 (3) authorization, but that error did not mandate reversal of conviction on a separately and validly indicted count.

Courts may require SCRAM alcohol-monitoring bracelets and related payment as probation conditions. If inability to pay is non-willful, courts must consider reasonable alternatives before incarceration.
Use of an anonymous jury without sufficient factual basis and without adequate mitigating safeguards was reversible error requiring a new trial.
